document_check.note: Tamaru Y, Inada S, Ideguchi N, Kagino S, Katsuhara Y, Higashi Y. Visual field-based reaction time as a novel indicator for early detection of mild cognitive impairment. Scientific Reports (2026) 16:2330, doi:10.1038/s41598-025-32034-6 (accepted 8 December 2025, copyright 2025). A cross-sectional comparison of 31 MCI and 43 cognitively healthy controls on a central and a UFOV reaction-time task: central RT did not differ (p = 0.228), UFOV RT did (p < 0.001), with a task-by-group interaction F(1,72) = 19.09. This matches the citation. The journal volume is dated 2026; 2025 is the online year.

cited_result: Reaction time to peripheral (UFOV) targets against central targets in 31 MCI and 43 cognitively healthy controls in one session: central RT 554.4 ms (SD 46.6) in controls against 568.5 ms (SD 52.6) in MCI, t = -1.22, p = 0.228; UFOV RT 580.3 ms (SD 44.9) against 638.6 ms (SD 38.4), t = -5.84, p < 0.001; mixed-design ANOVA task-by-group interaction F(1,72) = 19.09, p < 0.001, partial eta squared 0.210; the group effect on UFOV RT persisted in an ANCOVA with central RT as covariate. The logistic regression and ROC results (AUC 0.841, cut-off 598.1 ms) are a different result and are not appraised here.
tool_reason: The cited result is a between-group comparison of a behavioural measure (reaction time by task condition) in screening-defined MCI and control groups measured at one session, not a model's discrimination or a test's accuracy against a reference standard; the case-control checklist was not chosen because the paper recruited one pool of facility residents and classified them by screening scores rather than sampling cases and controls separately.

domains.domain: Item 1: Criteria for inclusion clearly defined
domains.rationale: The thresholds that define each group (controls: MoCA-J 26 or more and MMSE-J 28 to 30; MCI: MoCA-J 25 or less and MMSE-J 24 to 27) and the exclusions are stated. Gaps: no age limit is given, 'other neurological or medical conditions' is not operationalised, and the paper does not say what happened to residents whose two scores met neither group's thresholds (for example MoCA-J 25 or less with MMSE-J 28 to 30); the flow reports only five exclusions, all for exclusion criteria.

signalling.question: Were the criteria for inclusion in the sample clearly defined?
signalling.quote: Inclusion criteria for the HC group were a score of ≥ 26 on the Japanese version of the Montreal Cognitive Assessment (MoCA-J) and a score of 28–30 on the Japanese version of the Mini-Mental State Examination (MMSE-J). The MCI group included patients with MoCA-J scores ≤ 25 and MMSE-J scores 24–27

signalling.question: Were exclusion criteria stated?
signalling.quote: Exclusion criteria included: visual impairments, regular use of corrective glasses, cerebrovascular disease, or other neurological or medical conditions likely to affect cognitive or visual performance.

signalling.question: Was an age criterion stated?
signalling.quote: This cross-sectional study was conducted between 2024 and 2025 and included older adults residing in medical and nursing care facilities.

signalling.question: Is the handling of residents whose scores met neither group's thresholds stated?
signalling.quote: After excluding five individuals who met exclusion criteria, 74 patients were included in the final analysis

domains.domain: Item 2: Study subjects and setting described in detail
domains.rationale: The setting type (residents of medical and nursing care facilities), the period (2024 to 2025) and group age, sex, MoCA-J and MMSE-J are reported. The facilities are not named or counted, the recruitment route (consecutive, referred or volunteer) is not stated, and education, visual acuity and comorbidities are not reported. Education matters here because group membership rests on education-sensitive screening scores.

signalling.question: Were the setting and period reported?
signalling.quote: This cross-sectional study was conducted between 2024 and 2025 and included older adults residing in medical and nursing care facilities.

signalling.question: Are participant characteristics reported by group?
signalling.quote: 43 in the HC group (mean age: 72.2 ± 2.9 years; 21 males, 22 females; MoCA-J: 28.1 ± 1.0; MMSE-J: 29.4 ± 0.7)

signalling.question: Was the recruitment route described?
signalling.quote: A total of 79 participants were initially recruited.

signalling.question: Were education, visual function and comorbidities of the sample reported?
signalling.quote: Searched Methods, Table 1, Results and Discussion for years of education, visual acuity or comorbidities of the participants; none reported.

domains.domain: Item 3: Exposure (diagnostic group membership) measured validly and reliably
domains.rationale: Group membership rests on MoCA-J and MMSE-J cut-offs, which are established screening instruments applied to everyone in the same way. The paper does not say who administered them, whether examiners were trained or whether any reliability check was made, and the authors themselves describe the classification as falling short of the consensus clinical diagnosis they call the gold standard.

signalling.question: Was group membership established in a valid way?
signalling.quote: Third, MCI classification was based solely on MoCA and MMSE scores. While these are widely used screening tools, the gold standard typically involves a consensus clinical diagnosis incorporating multidisciplinary evaluation.

signalling.question: Were the examiners, administration procedure or reliability of the screening tests reported?
signalling.quote: Searched Methods and the author contributions for who administered MoCA-J and MMSE-J, examiner training and any reliability check; none reported.

signalling.question: Were both groups classified by the same procedure?
signalling.quote: Participants were classified into two groups: those with MCI (MCI group) and cognitively healthy controls (HC group).

domains.domain: Item 4: Objective, standard criteria used for measurement of the condition
domains.rationale: The criteria are objective numeric cut-offs, but they are screening thresholds (cited to the first author's earlier study), not a standard clinical definition of MCI: there is no cognitive complaint, functional assessment or clinical diagnosis, and the authors state that the classification is provisional.

signalling.question: Were objective, standard criteria used for measurement of the condition?
signalling.quote: The MCI group included patients with MoCA-J scores ≤ 25 and MMSE-J scores 24–27

signalling.question: Do the authors acknowledge that the classification falls short of standard diagnostic criteria?
signalling.quote: Therefore, our classification should be considered provisional, and future studies should validate UFOV-RT against consensus diagnostic criteria.

domains.rationale: The authors identify general response speed, alertness, fatigue and time-on-task as alternative explanations of the UFOV RT difference, and report age (compared between groups) and sex by group. Education, which affects both the screening scores that define the groups and speeded performance, is not identified, and peripheral visual function is addressed only by excluding 'visual impairments'.

signalling.question: Were confounding factors identified?
signalling.quote: To further examine whether the MCI–HC difference in U-RT could be explained by general response speed, an ANCOVA was conducted with U-RT as the dependent variable and C-RT as a covariate.

signalling.question: Were alertness, fatigue and time-on-task recognised as alternative explanations?
signalling.quote: The additional analyses reinforced that the prolonged U-RT observed in individuals with MCI cannot be attributed to general alertness or time-on-task effects.

signalling.question: Was education identified as a confounder?
signalling.quote: Searched Methods, Table 1, Results and Discussion for participants' education; the only mention of education is general, in the Introduction (screening methods 'often influenced by educational background'), not as a variable of this sample.

domains.domain: Item 6: Strategies to deal with confounding stated
domains.rationale: The within-subject design (central task as a baseline), the task-by-group interaction and the ANCOVA with central RT address general response speed, and visual impairment is handled by exclusion. Age and sex are not adjusted for (mean ages 72.2 and 73.4, p = 0.12; males 58% of the MCI group against 49% of controls), education is not measured, and the task order was fixed (central always first, the UFOV task four times as long). A group difference in fatigue or time-on-task is therefore confounded with the UFOV condition and could not be analysed, because the software kept only the overall mean UFOV RT. The strategies are partial.

signalling.question: Were strategies to deal with confounding factors stated?
signalling.quote: In addition, an ANCOVA was performed using C-RT as a covariate to examine group differences in U-RT while controlling for baseline response speed.

signalling.question: Were age, sex and education accounted for in the group comparison?
signalling.quote: Reaction time met normality assumptions and was analyzed using an independent samples t-test.

signalling.question: Was task order counterbalanced or time-on-task controlled?
signalling.quote: To minimize potential carry-over effects, the central visual field task was always presented first, followed by the UFOV task.

signalling.question: Could time-on-task effects be examined?
signalling.quote: Consequently, we could not directly examine time-on-task effects.

domains.domain: Item 7: Outcomes (reaction time) measured validly and reliably
domains.rationale: RT was recorded automatically as the latency from stimulus onset to button press, with the same equipment, trial timing and task order for every participant, so differential measurement between groups is unlikely. However, the stimulus software was custom-built for the study and no validation of its timing or test-retest reliability is reported; it output only the mean RT per task, so the handling of anticipations, outliers and trials in which gaze left the fixation point (visual orienting frequency, median 3 against 2, p = 0.052) is not reported; the investigators collected the data and blinding to group is not stated. The task is a peripheral detection task with 2 s stimuli rather than the standardised UFOV test.

signalling.question: Was the outcome defined and measured in a valid way?
signalling.quote: Reaction time was recorded using a USB-connected response button (model USBSWP; TECHNOTOOLS, Japan). Reaction time was defined as the latency between stimulus onset and button press.

signalling.question: Was the measurement system validated or its reliability reported?
signalling.quote: Stimulus presentation was controlled by a custom-built VRAS.

signalling.question: Was the measurement procedure the same for all participants?
signalling.quote: All assessments were conducted with participants seated in a stable, upright position.

signalling.question: Was the handling of individual trials (anticipations, misses, gaze shifts) in the mean RT reported?
signalling.quote: Fifth, the stimulus presentation software provided only the overall mean RT for the 80 UFOV trials, which precluded analysis across smaller blocks of 20 trials.

signalling.question: Was fixation enforced during the peripheral task?
signalling.quote: visual orienting frequency (VOF), defined as the number of gaze shifts away from the central fixation point toward peripheral stimuli.

signalling.question: Was RT recorded without knowledge of group membership?
signalling.quote: Y.T., Y.H., S.K., and Y.K. participated in data collection.

domains.rationale: The cited comparison uses t-tests after Shapiro-Wilk checks, a mixed-design ANOVA whose task-by-group interaction tests the question directly, and an ANCOVA with central RT. The contrast (UFOV RT but not central RT differs) is stated as the first hypothesis in the Introduction, although no protocol or registration is cited. Caveats: no correction across the seven group comparisons (the cited results are p < 0.001 or null), no report of variance or regression-slope homogeneity checks, ANCOVA F statistics with df (1,72) where one covariate and one group factor on 74 participants leave 71 error df, and a UFOV RT Cohen's d of -1.17 that does not agree with the reported means, SDs and t (these give about 1.38). None of these changes the direction or significance of the cited result.

signalling.question: Was the analysis appropriate for the cited comparison?
signalling.quote: A mixed-design ANOVA was conducted with task condition (C-RT vs. U-RT) as a within-subject factor and group (HC vs. MCI) as a between-subject factor.

signalling.question: Were distributional assumptions checked?
signalling.quote: The Shapiro–Wilk test assessed the normality of each variable. Reaction time met normality assumptions and was analyzed using an independent samples t-test.

signalling.question: Was the cited contrast specified in advance of the results?
signalling.quote: We hypothesized that reaction time in the UFOV condition, but not the central condition, would significantly differ between groups

signalling.question: Was correction for multiple comparisons applied?
signalling.quote: A significance level of p < 0.05 was used for all tests.

signalling.question: Are the reported statistics internally consistent?
signalling.quote: group difference (t = − 5.84, p < 0.001, Cohen’s d = − 1.17)

applicability.rationale: Residents of medical and nursing care facilities assessed with Japanese-language instruments, in a narrow age band (group means 72.2 and 73.4, SD 2.9 and 3.9), excluding anyone with a visual impairment or who regularly uses corrective glasses; group mean MoCA-J scores (28.1 and 22.7) lie well away from the 25/26 threshold.

MCI is a screening-score category (MoCA-J 25 or less and MMSE-J 24 to 27) without clinical diagnosis, which the authors call provisional; the result compares screen-positive with screen-negative residents rather than clinically diagnosed MCI with controls.

The 'UFOV' task is a custom peripheral detection task (2 s stimuli at four fixed locations 20 cm from centre at 1 m, on a 2D monitor, always after the central task) rather than the standardised UFOV test, so the result may not transfer to other UFOV implementations.

overall: Some concerns (JBI analytical cross-sectional: item 4 No; items 2, 3, 6 and 7 Unclear; items 1, 5 and 8 Yes)
overall_rationale: None of the four items that the review's rule treats as decisive (5, 6, 7 and 8) is No, but items 6 and 7 are Unclear, so the result cannot be low. The concerns are the screening-only definition of MCI (item 4 No, item 3 Unclear), partial handling of confounding (no adjustment for age, sex or education, and a fixed task order that confounds the UFOV condition with time-on-task, which the authors could not analyse), and a custom RT system with no reported validation and unreported trial handling. The within-subject contrast and the ANCOVA on central RT do address generic slowing, the main alternative explanation of the cited interaction.
